description: Excerpts featuring Fr. Robert Mary Clement and John Darcy Noble's participation in the first Christopher Street Liberation Day March. title: Jet Magazine coverage of the Church of the Beloved Disciple's first widely publicized Holy Union ceremony
description: Published on May 13, 1971, this Jet magazine article brought national attention to the Church of the Beloved Disciple and its pioneering ministry to LGBTQ Christians. The feature reported on the Holy Union of Joan B. Kearse and Bobbi Jean Sanchez, a ceremony originally celebrated by Fr. Robert M. Clement in July 1970 at the Church of the Holy Apostles, an Episcopal parish on West 28th Street in Manhattan's Chelsea neighborhood where the church was renting space for its services. Attended by nearly 300 people, the service became one of the earliest same-sex Christian union ceremonies in NYC to receive widespread media coverage. The article introduced a broad audience to Clement's ministry and the Church of the Beloved Disciple as a pioneering religious community affirming same-sex relationships.

title: New York Post coverage of the Church of the Beloved Disciple's Holy Union ceremonies
description: As public attention to the Church of the Beloved Disciple's pioneering Holy Union ceremonies grew following the first public cememony in July 1970, the New York Post reported that Fr. Robert M. Clement intentionally described the rites as Holy Unions rather than marriages, acknowledging that New York law did not recognize same-sex marriage. The article explained that the ceremonies closely followed the structure of a traditional Christian wedding while distinguishing them from civil marriage. It also documented the legal controversy surrounding the services, including threats of prosecution by New York City officials, highlighting the growing tension between religious innovation, LGBTQ rights, and the law.

title: National Recognition in Catholic World
description: The June 1971 issue of Catholic World featured Robert M. Clement on its cover carrying the sign, "Gay People, This Is Your Church," during New York's second Christopher Street Liberation Day March. Published less than two years after the Stonewall uprising, the image brought national attention to Clement's emerging ministry and to one of the first openly LGBTQ-affirming Catholic congregations in the United States. The cover illustrates how the Church of the Beloved Disciple quickly became a visible symbol of the growing movement to reconcile Christian faith with LGBTQ identity.

title: Interview with Randy Wicker
object_transcript:
Transcript: timestamp 1:04-2:53 [edited for clarity]: 
Wicker: Hi I'm Randy Wicker, today we're talking to Father Robert Clement of the Church of the Beloved Disciple. Father Clement, what type of church is the Church of the Beloved Disciple? 
Clement: Like all churches, it's basically first a church for everyone, but our congregation is primarily gay, I'd say 90%.
Wicker: See now I understand that some of the services you perform, namely the service of Holy Union came under a great deal of criticism and attack recently.
Clement: Well it caused some consternation, surprisingly to us because this is a church rite in the sense of, I mean a church ceremony that's natural and logical outgrowth of our own people, our community that we serve. People are in love and they have a right to the expression of this love and the church acknowledging it is a beautiful thing.
Wicker: Well is this a gay marriage?
Clement: No, we don't use the term marriage because that implies a legal concept and a marriage certificate and Bureau of Vital Statistics and we are interested in a church concept which is spiritual. People pledging their love together in the eyes of God and asking the blessing of God and that's what we're all about. But this was misinterpreted and when publicity came out in the New York Post, the article said about gay marriages which is not our concept, but I understand how it caused this confusion. Then the city clerk got into it and started saying we were performing illegal marriages and so on, which was rather far from our minds, but did get into some confusion. Of course we believe this is something that is valuable for all mankind to affirm their love and especially for gay people in in our community
Wicker: Okay thank you Reverend Clement and now we’re going to go to the GAA Firehouse pick up with the GAA people and continue to the marriage bureau where I understand an engagement party is due to be held this is Randy Wicker.

title: Gay Activist alliance ZAP
description: General information about the Gay activist alliance ZAP with links to Youtube videos. New York’s City Clerk Herman Katz became incensed over the publicity of a same-sex “illegal marriage” being officiate by Clement in April 1971. Katz threatened legal action against Clement for performing what he called mock marriages. In response, the Gay Activists Alliance held one of its most famous and creative zaps, an engagement party for two same-sex couples, complete with wedding cake, on June 4, 1971, at the Marriage Bureau in the Municipal Building.

title: Holy Union ceremony celebrated by Fr. Robert Mary Clement, early 1970s
description: This photograph captures one of the Church of the Beloved Disciple's Holy Union ceremonies, officiated by Fr. Robert Mary Clement before a large congregation at an unidentified location. Following a liturgy modeled closely on the Christian marriage rite, the couple exchanged vows and rings as the community gathered to witness and bless their covenant. Throughout the 1970s, these public ceremonies offered LGBTQ couples a sacramental affirmation of their relationships decades before civil marriage equality became a reality in the United States.

title: Service of Holy Union for John and Israel
description: Fr. John Darcy Noble officiates the Holy Union of John C. Fout and Israel at the Church of the Beloved Disciple, 348 West 14th Street, New York City. By the mid-1970s, the Church's Holy Union liturgy had become a well-established sacramental rite through which same-sex couples celebrated their love for one another.

title: The Kiss of Peace following the Holy Union ceremony
description: After exchanging vows and rings, John C. Fout and Israel seal their covenant with a kiss as Fr. John Darcy Noble and assisting clergy look on. The public blessing of same-sex couples formed the heart of the Church of the Beloved Disciple's ministry, offering LGBTQ Christians a sacramental affirmation of their relationships nearly four decades before marriage equality became the law of the United States.

title: Celebration following a Holy Union ceremony at the Church of the Beloved Disciple
description: After the liturgy, a newly united couple shares wine and cake at the reception celebrating their Holy Union. Such gatherings were an integral part of the Church of the Beloved Disciple's ministry, affirming same-sex relationships not only through sacramental rites but also through the communal rituals of hospitality, fellowship, and joyful celebration that traditionally followed Christian weddings.

title: Holy Union of Archbishop Robert Mary Clement and Fr. John Darcy Noble
description: Pastor Troy Perry, founder of the Metropolitan Community Church, officiates the Holy Union of Robert Mary Clement and John Darcy Noble at the Performing Garage, 33 Wooster Street in Manhattan's SoHo district. The ceremony was relocated after Fr. Robert Weeks, rector of the Church of the Holy Apostles in Chelsea, refused to allow the service to be held at Holy Apostles because of concerns over the anticipated media attention.

title: Perry, Clement, and Noble celebrating
description: Pastor Troy Perry, Father Robert Mary Clement, and John Darcy Noble outside the Performing Garage following the Holy Union ceremony. Standing beneath the entrance to 33 Wooster Street in Manhattan's SoHo neighborhood, Troy Perry (center), founder of the Metropolitan Community Church, celebrates with Robert Mary Clement (left) and John Darcy Noble (right) after officiating their Holy Union. Although the Metropolitan Community Church and the Church of the Beloved Disciple were sometimes viewed as competing ministries within the emerging LGBTQ Christian movement, Perry and Clement maintained a warm personal friendship and shared a commitment to providing spiritual community for lesbian and gay Christians during the formative years of the gay liberation movement.

title: Restored Portrait of Fr. Robert Mary Clement
description: This digitally restored photograph depicts the Rev. Robert Mary Clement before the founding of the Church of the Beloved Disciple. At the time, Clement was serving as a parish priest of the Polish National Catholic Church in Perth Amboy, New Jersey. In 1968 he founded the American Orthodox Church of the United States (Western Orthodox). In 1970, he established the Church of the Beloved Disciple parish as the first sacramental church in New York City established specifically to minister openly to gay and lesbian Christians. Clement's ministry would become a pioneering force in the movement for LGBTQ inclusion within historic Christian sacramental traditions.

title: Certificate of Priestly Ordination of Robert Mary Clement
description: This document certifies the ordination of Robert Mary Clement to the sacred order of the priesthood on 7 August 1948. Written in Latin, the certificate was issued under the authority of Bishop William H. F. Brothers, Archbishop of the Old Catholic Church in North America. The text attests that Clement was examined, found qualified according to ecclesiastical requirements, and promoted to the priesthood ad titulum missionis (for missionary service). The certificate was issued at Woodstock, New York, on 8 August 1948 and bears the signatures of the ordaining prelate and ecclesiastical officials together with an embossed church seal. The document provides primary evidence of Clement's clerical status, ordination date, ordaining jurisdiction, and apostolic lineage within the independent Catholic movement in mid-twentieth-century North America.

title: American Orthodox Church of the United States (Western Orthodox) Articles of Incorporation 1969
description: This Certificate of Incorporation, executed on March 12, 1969, formally established the American Orthodox Church of the United States (Western Orthodox) as a religious corporation under New York law and named Robert Mary Clement as its presiding officer. The document outlines the church's mission, governance, and authority to organize dioceses, ordained clergy, consecrate bishops, and establish churches and charitable institutions throughout the United States.

title: Parade flyer for the first NYC Pride Parade
description: Flyer for the first NYC Pride Parade, then called the Christopher Street Liberation Day March, held in New York, New York, on June 28, 1970, to commemorate the first anniversary of the Stonewall Riots.

title: "Gay People, This Is Your Church"
description: Robert M. Clement and John Darcy Noble stand in Sheep Meadow following the first Christopher Street Liberation Day March on June 28, 1970, beneath a hand-painted sign proclaiming, "Gay People, This Is Your Church." Earlier that day, Clement carried this sign in the march while Noble distributed leaflets announcing their forthcoming inaugural public Mass. Created less than one year after the Stonewall uprising, the sign publicly proclaimed the emergence of an affirming sacramental ministry for lesbian and gay people that would soon develop into the Church of the Beloved Disciple. This restored photograph preserves one of the earliest surviving public images of Clement and Noble's ministry and documents a pioneering declaration that LGBTQ Christians could participate fully in the sacramental life of the Church without concealing their identities.

title: Clement celebrating first public mass in New York City 1
description: On July 19, 1970, Father Robert M. Clement celebrated the first public Mass of the newly founded Church of the Beloved Disciple at the Church of the Holy Apostles in Manhattan. Attended by more than 500 people, the liturgy offered an unprecedented public expression of sacramental worship affirming the spiritual lives of LGBTQ people and marked a watershed in the history of queer Christianity. The service attracted national media attention and established the Church of the Beloved Disciple as one of the earliest LGBTQ-affirming sacramental communities in the United States.

title: St. John the Beloved at the Stonewall Inn during the 1973 New York City Pride March
description: Archbishop Robert Mary Clement stands outside the Stonewall Inn on Christopher Street with members of the Church of the Beloved Disciple carrying a processional banner depicting St. John the Beloved during the Fourth Annual Christopher Street Liberation Day March and Rally on June 24, 1973.

title: Church of the Beloved Disciple at the 1973 New York City Pride March
description: Archbishop Robert Mary Clement leads members of the Church of the Beloved Disciple during the Fourth Annual Christopher Street Liberation Day March and Rally on June 24, 1973. Flanking the processional banner of St. John the Beloved are Fr. John (left) and Fr. Leo (right), who carry the banner through the streets of Manhattan. Clothed in liturgical vestments, the congregation offered a striking public witness that LGBTQ people belonged fully within the sacramental life of the Church.

title: Church of the Beloved Disciple at the 1974 New York City Pride March
description: Members of the Church of the Beloved Disciple process through Midtown Manhattan during the Fifth Annual Christopher Street Liberation Day March on June 30, 1974. Marching beneath processional crosses, banners, and the church's heraldic standard, the congregation transformed the annual Pride march into a public act of Christian witness, proclaiming that LGBTQ people belonged fully within the sacramental life of the Church. By 1974, the Church of the Beloved Disciple had become one of the most visible religious organizations participating in New York City's Pride celebrations, bringing liturgy, sacred art, and public faith into the heart of the growing gay liberation movement.

title: After the 1974 New York City Pride March in Central Park
description: Fr. Leo speaks with a member of the Church of the Beloved Disciple in Sheep Meadow following the Fifth Annual Christopher Street Liberation Day March on June 30, 1974. Surrounding them are the church's processional banners and heraldic standard, while the congregant wears a distinctive silver cross designed by Fr. Leo and adopted by members of the congregation as a symbol of their shared faith and community.

title: Eucharistic Catholic Church banner at the 1974 New York City Pride March
description: Carried by members of the Church of the Beloved Disciple during the Fifth Annual Christopher Street Liberation Day March on June 30, 1974, this processional banner features heraldic imagery created by the Church of the Beloved Disciple in honor of the Eucharistic Catholic Church, founded by Archbishop George Augustine Hyde in 1946. By designing and publicly displaying a coat of arms for the Eucharistic Catholic Church, the congregation affirmed its spiritual and historical continuity with Hyde's pioneering ministry. The banner proclaimed the Church of the Beloved Disciple's understanding of itself as the successor to the Eucharistic Catholic Church, continuing its mission of providing a sacramental home for LGBTQ Christians within the historic Catholic tradition.

title: Church of the Beloved Disciple in the 1975 Pride March
description: Clergy of the Church of the Beloved Disciple process ahead of the congregation's float during the Sixth Annual Gay Pride Day March (Gay Liberation Day) in New York City on June 29, 1975. From left to right are Fr. Leo (partially visible), Fr. John (center), and Bishop Robert Mary Clement (wearing the mitre), accompanied by unidentified acolytes and cross-bearers. Behind them, the Church of the Beloved Disciple's float, designed as a processional chapel, affirmed the congregation's conviction that LGBTQ Christians belonged fully within the sacramental life of the Church and brought liturgical worship into one of the nation's most visible public celebrations of gay liberation.

title: Church of the Beloved Disciple Pride Float 1975
description: A closer view of the Church of the Beloved Disciple's float during the Sixth Annual Gay Pride Day March (Gay Liberation Day) in New York City on June 29, 1975. Decorated as a processional chapel and crowned with the sign "Beloved Disciple Parish," the float featured the congregation's heraldic arms and iconography, visually expressing its Catholic sacramental identity. The individuals on the float are presently unidentified, but their white albs and distinctive crosses reflected the liturgical character of the congregation's public witness.

title: Pride Parade Float 1976
description: The Church of the Beloved Disciple's float at the Seventh Annual Christopher Street Liberation Day March commemorated the thirtieth anniversary (1946–1976) of Archbishop George Augustine Hyde's Eucharistic Catholic Church. Featuring congregation members portraying Archbishop George Augustine Hyde and Bishop Robert Mary Clement, the float presented the Church of the Beloved Disciple as the spiritual successor to Hyde's pioneering ministry. The central heraldic emblem, created by the Church of the Beloved Disciple to represent the Eucharistic Catholic Church, symbolized that continuity, while the prominent inscription "World's First Gay Church" proclaimed the congregation's understanding that Hyde's church was the earliest sacramental Christian community in the United States established to minister openly to gay men and lesbians. Through this public display, the Church of the Beloved Disciple celebrated and extended that legacy as an LGBTQ-affirming Catholic ministry in New York City.

title: Church of the Beloved Disciple Pride Float.
description: The Church of the Beloved Disciple's float during a New York City Gay Pride march, circa late 1970s - early 1980s, featured clergy in episcopal vestments beneath the congregation's distinctive floral cross. Prominently displayed were the coat of arms of the Church of the Beloved Disciple, emblazoned on purple processional banners that had become a recognizable symbol of the congregation's public ministry.

title: Quentin Crisp Joins the Church of the Beloved Disciple at New York Pride
description: English writer and gay icon Quentin Crisp (center) rides with Fr. John Darcy Noble (left) and Bishop Robert Mary Clement (right) in the Church of the Beloved Disciple's lead convertible during the 13th Annual Gay Pride Day March in New York City on June 27, 1982.

title: Church of the Beloved Disciple at the New York City Pride March
description: Members of the Church of the Beloved Disciple march beneath the congregation's name banner and the heraldic standard during New York City's annual Pride Parade, circa late 1970s - early 1980s. By this time, the church had become a familiar presence in Pride marches, returning each year with banners, vestments, and religious symbols that proclaimed the compatibility of Christian faith and LGBTQ identity. The procession embodied the church's enduring mission to make visible a sacramental tradition in which LGBTQ people could worship openly, celebrate their relationships, and participate fully in the life of the Church.

title: Church of the Beloved Disciple at the New York City Pride March.
description: Members of the Church of the Beloved Disciple carry the congregation's banner during New York City's annual Pride Parade, circa late 1970s - early 1980s. The church marched each year as an openly Christian presence within the LGBTQ movement, proclaiming that gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender people belonged fully within the life of the Church. While clergy often processed in liturgical vestments and carried crosses and banners, lay members walked alongside them, demonstrating that the Church of the Beloved Disciple was both a worshiping community and a visible participant in the ongoing struggle for equality, dignity, and religious inclusion.

title: First service in the churches second location - Moravian Church on Lexington Avenue
description: On November 1, 1972, the Church of the Beloved Disciple held its first service at the Moravian Church on Lexington Avenue, marking the congregation's second worship location since its founding.

title: Third home at the West Side Discussion Group
description: After being asked to leave the Moravian Church, the Church of the Beloved Disciple found a new home at the West Side Discussion Group, where it celebrated worship in the fall of 1973. The congregation's move reflects the challenges faced by LGBTQ-affirming religious communities in securing stable worship space during the early years of the gay liberation movement. Despite repeated displacement, the church continued to celebrate the Eucharist and expand its ministry, demonstrating the resilience and determination of its members to create a spiritual home for LGBTQ people.

title: West Side Discussion Group Center
description: NYC LGBTQ Historic Sites website with details about the West Side Discussion Group Center.

title: Procession to new building
description: This New York Times article documents the Church of the Beloved Disciple's public procession through Manhattan to its newly renovated church at 348 West 14th Street. Accompanied by clergy, servers, and processional crosses, the congregation carried the Blessed Sacrament from its previous worship site to its first permanent home, marking a milestone in the history of LGBTQ religious life in New York City. The newspaper's coverage reflects the growing public visibility of the church and its emergence as a recognized presence within both the city's religious landscape and the gay liberation movement.

title: Clement blesses new building
description: Before celebrating the first Mass in the congregation's newly renovated church, Father Robert M. Clement blesses the entrance to the Church of the Beloved Disciple with the Eucharist. Surrounded by clergy, parishioners, and the church's distinctive processional banners, the ceremony marked the dedication of the congregation's first permanent home after years of worshiping in borrowed spaces. The blessing inaugurated a new chapter in the life of one of the nation's earliest openly LGBTQ-affirming Catholic communities.

title: External view of church building after remodel
description: Following an extensive renovation by parishioners, 348 West 14th Street became the permanent home of the Church of the Beloved Disciple and the center of its ministry to New York City's LGBTQ community. Dedicated in October 1973, the former commercial building was transformed into a church through the labor and financial support of its members, creating one of the first permanently owned houses of worship established by an openly LGBTQ Christian congregation in New York City. From this sanctuary, the church celebrated the Eucharist, ordained clergy, and became a center of LGBTQ religious life and independent Catholic ministry in New York.

title: Close up of external view of church building after remodel
description: The renovated façade of the Church of the Beloved Disciple at 348 West 14th Street, the congregation's permanent home from 1973 until 1983. Purchased and restored through the labor and generosity of parishioners, the building became one of the first permanently owned houses of worship established by an openly LGBTQ Christian congregation in the United States. For nearly a decade, it served as a sanctuary for worship, community, and pioneering LGBTQ religious life in New York City.

title: Pontifical Mass on Easter Sunday 1976 1
description: Viewed from the rear of the sanctuary, Archbishop Robert M. Clement with Fr. Leo (on his left) and Fr. John (on his right) processing to the altar before celebrates the Pontifical Mass of Easter Sunday before a congregation filling the Church of the Beloved Disciple. The elevated altar, adorned with lilies, candles, and a suspended crucifix, provided a setting for one of the most solemn liturgies of the Christian year, celebrated according to the ceremonial traditions of the Catholic Church. This image captures the church at the height of its liturgical life, when its permanent home had become both a place of worship and a refuge for LGBTQ Christians seeking a sacramental community. Takes place at the 348 West 14th street location.

title: Pontifical Mass on Easter Sunday 1976 2
description: Archbishop Robert M. Clement with Fr. Leo (on his left) and Fr. John (on his right) celebrates the Pontifical Mass of Easter Sunday before a congregation gathered in the Church of the Beloved Disciple's permanent sanctuary. Surrounded by clergy and elaborate Easter floral decorations, the solemn liturgy exemplified the church's commitment to the full ceremonial tradition of Catholic worship while serving an openly LGBTQ-affirming community. Takes place at the 348 West 14th street location.

title: Carved Sanctuary Crucifix (ca. 1968–1970)
description: This carved wooden crucifix (seen hanging above the altar in the preceeding pictures), created by artist Robert Robbins, served as the principal cross of the Church of the Beloved Disciple throughout its history. First displayed at the congregation's inaugural Eucharist in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Manhattan, it remained a constant presence as the community moved to successive worship spaces, ultimately hanging in the sanctuary at 348 West 14th Street. Depicting the risen and glorified Christ with outstretched arms and visible wounds, the crucifix embodied the church's theology of resurrection, welcome, and reconciliation.

title: Processional Crucifix
description: Carved by the noted ecclesiastical sculptor Robert ("Robbie") Robbins, this processional crucifix was commissioned for the Church of the Beloved Disciple and served as one of the principal symbols of the congregation's public and liturgical life. Carried in solemn liturgies, feast day processions, and in public marches, the cross reflects Robbins's distinctive synthesis of medieval and modern forms. Christ is depicted as the crucified King, crowned and reigning from the Tree of Life, while the interlaced Celtic ornament that fills the cross evokes the eternal and unbroken life of God. Robbins, whose work adorned numerous Roman Catholic and Anglo-Catholic churches along the East Coast, created this crucifix specifically for the Church of the Beloved Disciple.

title: Fr. Leo censing
description: Leo M. Joseph census the altar during the celebration of the Eucharist in the Church of the Beloved Disciple's permanent sanctuary. The use of incense, richly colored vestments, and traditional ceremonial reflected the congregation's commitment to historic Catholic worship, demonstrating that LGBTQ affirmation and liturgical tradition could coexist within a fully sacramental community. This photograph captures the reverence and beauty that characterized the church's liturgical life during its years at 348 West 14th Street.

title: Fr. Leo reading with view of vestments
description: Father Leo M. Joseph proclaims the Eucharistic prayers vested in an ornate chasuble embroidered with the Agnus Dei(Lamb of God) and Eucharistic symbols. The richly decorated vestments, many designed by Father Leo, expressed the Church of the Beloved Disciple's conviction that the dignity and beauty of Catholic worship belonged fully within an LGBTQ-affirming community. This close view highlights the church's careful preservation of traditional liturgical artistry alongside its pioneering ministry of inclusion.

title: Fr. Leo and Fr. John with two unknown acolytes
description: Father Leo M. Joseph (left) and Father John Noble (right) prepare for the celebration of the Eucharist with two acolytes inside the Church of the Beloved Disciple's permanent sanctuary. The church preserved the richness of the Catholic liturgical tradition through solemn ceremonial worship while offering an affirming spiritual home for LGBTQ Christians. This intimate moment behind the altar captures the collaborative ministry of clergy and servers that sustained one of the earliest openly LGBTQ-affirming sacramental congregations in the United States.

title: Mass for Gay pride march 1975
description: Father John Noble (left), Father Robert M. Clement (center), and Father Leo M. Joseph (right) celebrate a special Eucharist in honor of New York City's annual Gay Pride March in June 1975. For the Church of the Beloved Disciple, the Mass was both a preparation for public witness and an affirmation that LGBTQ identity and Catholic faith were inseparable. Following the liturgy, the congregation processed through Manhattan in clerical vestments, carrying banners, crosses, and the Blessed Sacrament in one of the earliest public expressions of LGBTQ-affirming sacramental worship in the United States.

title: Marian Shrine
description: A side chapel dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary provided a quiet place for personal prayer within the Church of the Beloved Disciple. Centered on an icon painted by John Darcy Noble, the shrine was adorned with candles, flowers, and votive lights, reflecting the congregation's enduring practice of traditional Catholic devotion. Like the church's public processions and liturgical celebrations, the shrine affirmed that contemplative prayer and Marian piety remained central to the spiritual life of this pioneering LGBTQ-affirming community.

title: Icon of the Virgin and Child
description: This icon of the Virgin and Child, painted by John Darcy Noble, served as the focal point of the Church of the Beloved Disciple's Marian shrine. Drawing upon the visual language of Eastern Christian iconography while reflecting Noble's own artistic vision, the image depicts Mary tenderly embracing the Christ Child as an expression of divine compassion and maternal care. The icon became one of the congregation's most cherished devotional works, inviting prayer and contemplation while embodying the church's commitment to beauty, tradition, and sacred art.

title: Our Lady of the Church of the Beloved Disciple
description: The Church of the Beloved Disciple's statue of the Blessed Virgin Mary was richly adorned with embroidered garments, a lace veil, fresh flowers, and a floral crown prepared for the church's liturgical seasons and Marian feasts. Displayed within the sanctuary and carried in annual processions, the image reflected the congregation's deep devotion to Mary as a symbol of compassion, fidelity, and hope. Through such traditional expressions of piety, the church affirmed its place within the historic Catholic devotional tradition.

title: Our Lady of the Church of the Beloved Disciple
description: Seen in profile, the church's statue of the Blessed Virgin Mary is dressed in elaborate vestments and crowned with flowers in preparation for a public procession. Carried through the streets on the Feast of the Assumption and other Marian celebrations, the image linked the Church of the Beloved Disciple to centuries of Catholic devotional practice while making that tradition visibly present within New York City's LGBTQ community. The statue became one of the congregation's most cherished symbols of continuity, beauty, and sacred presence.

title: Our Lady and the Christ Child
description: This restored view depicts the Church of the Beloved Disciple's principal Marian statue holding the Christ Child, both crowned with floral wreaths for a feast day celebration. The image occupied a place of honor within the sanctuary and was carefully decorated by members of the congregation as an expression of reverence and beauty. It served as a focal point for prayer throughout the liturgical year and accompanied the parish during outdoor Marian processions through the streets of Manhattan.

title: Stained glass window with St John the Beloved
description: Designed collaboratively by Leo Joseph and John Darcy Noble and executed in England using traditional stained-glass techniques, this window was commissioned for the Church of the Beloved Disciple and imported to New York in 1970. Depicting St. John the Beloved, the church's patron and namesake, it was installed in a side chapel of the congregation's permanent sanctuary in 1973 as a visual expression of its commitment to historic Catholic tradition and an affirming sacramental ministry. The shrine also housed the relics of the Eucharistic Catholic Church, entrusted by Bishop George Augustine Hyde, who founded that church in Atlanta in 1946. By presenting these relics to Bishop Robert Mary Clement and the Church of the Beloved Disciple, Hyde recognized the congregation as the spiritual successor to the Eucharistic Catholic Church, linking its ministry in Manhattan to an earlier independent Catholic tradition and affirming its continuing apostolic mission.

title: Processional Banner of St. John the Beloved
description: This painted processional banner depicts St. John the Beloved, patron of the Church of the Beloved Disciple, in a style derived from the church's celebrated stained-glass window. Mounted on purple felt with decorative tassels, the banner was carried in liturgical processions, ecumenical events, and New York City public marches, including Pride celebrations and other outdoor religious observances. Designed collaboratively by Leo and John Darcy Noble, it became one of the congregation's most recognizable visual emblems, appearing in numerous photographs documenting the church's public witness throughout the 1970s.

title: Commemorative church greeting card
description: The front of this devotional card features the Church of the Beloved Disciple's image of St. John the Beloved, reproduced from the stained-glass window designed collaboratively by Leo Joseph and John Darcy Noble. Commissioned in England and imported to New York in 1970, the window became the visual emblem of the congregation and frequently appeared on printed liturgical materials, prayer cards, and church publications. Measuring approximately 4.25 × 6 inches, the folded card welcomed visitors while expressing the church's identity through the figure of its patron saint.

title: The Ordination of Fathers Leo M. Joseph and John Darcy Noble
description: Bishop Thomas J. Fehérváry ordains Father Leo M. Joseph and Father John Darcy Noble to the Catholic priesthood at his chapel in Montreal, Quebec, on April 20, 1974, while Robert Mary Clement assists as deacon. Celebrated as the first two openly gay men to be ordained as Catholic priests without concealing their sexual orientation, Joseph and Noble would soon become central figures in the ministry of the Church of the Beloved Disciple in New York City. Their ordination by the Hungarian Mariavite Old Catholic bishop, whose apostolic succession traced through the Polish Mariavite Church, provided the sacramental foundation for a ministry dedicated to serving LGBTQ Christians. Less than six months later, Clement himself would be consecrated Bishop of New York, and together the three clergy would help build one of the earliest sacramental communities for gay and lesbian Christians in New York City.

title: "Two gay men ordained priests"
description: Press release issued by the Church of the Beloved Disciple, authored by Robert Bradley, announcing the ordination of John Darcy Noble and Leo M. Joseph on April 20, 1974. The statement proclaimed the ordinations as the first known instance of two openly acknowledged gay men being ordained to the apostolic priesthood with the full knowledge and acceptance of their sexual orientation by all participants. It also introduced the Church of the Beloved Disciple to the wider public as an apostolic Christian community serving New York City's gay community and invited readers to attend its services at 348 West 14th Street in Manhattan.

title: Opening Pages of Bishop Robert Mary Clement's Consecration Service Booklet
description: The opening pages of the official program for the Ceremony of Consecration of The Most Reverend Robert M. Clement as Bishop of New York of the Eucharistic Catholic Church, held at Metropolitan-Duane Church, New York City, on Sunday, October 6, 1974. The booklet includes Bishop Clement's official portrait, the order of service, and the names of the principal participants, including Archbishop Richard A. Marchenna, who served as consecrator, and co-consecrators Bishop Emile R. Fairfield (who was ultiameytly unable to attend the concecration) and Bishop Martin Luther Williams.

title: Consecration of Clement. Clement kneeling with Gospel Book across his shoulders
description: Robert Mary Clement kneels before the altar with the Book of the Gospels resting across his shoulders during the central rite of episcopal consecration at Metropolitan-Duane United Methodist Church in New York City on October 6, 1974. He was consecrated bishop by Archbishop Richard Arthur Marchenna, assisted by Bishop Martin Luther Williams, with Rev. Albert J. Berube of the North American Old Roman Catholic Church (Archdiocese of New York) also participating in the ceremony. At left, Fr. John Darcy Noble is seen from behind, while Fr. Leo Joseph stands to the right of Archbishop Marchenna. An unidentified acolyte supports the Gospel Book during the rite. Widely publicized and televised in New York City, the consecration was presented as the first public episcopal consecration of an openly gay bishop in the United States.

title: Close up of Marchenna at the Consecration of Clement
description: Archbishop Richard Arthur Marchenna consecrating Robert Mary Clement on Sunday, October 6, 1974 at the Metropolitan-Duane United Methodist Church, New York City.

title: Metropolitan-Duane United Methodist Church
description: NYC LGBTQ Historic Sites website with details about the Metropolitan-Duane United Methodist Church

title: Consecration Procession through Greenwich Village.
description: Bishop Robert Mary Clement leads the solemn procession from Metropolitan-Duane United Methodist Church at 201 West 13th Street to the Church of the Beloved Disciple at 348 West 14th Street following his episcopal consecration on October 6, 1974. At his side walks Archbishop Martin Luther Williams of the African Orthodox Church, while clergy and supporters follow behind. The public procession through the streets of Greenwich Village visibly proclaimed the Church of the Beloved Disciple's apostolic identity, carrying the celebration of Clement's consecration beyond the sanctuary and into the neighborhood it served.

title: An Ecumenical Procession of Bishops and Clergy
description: Clergy and bishops process westward through Manhattan following the consecration of Bishop Robert Mary Clement. The procession includes Archbishop Martin Luther Williams, Archbishop Richard Arthur Marchenna, Bishop Robert Clement, and clergy of the Church of the Beloved Disciple, together with supporters from several independent Catholic and Orthodox jurisdictions. Their participation reflected the broad ecumenical relationships that sustained the Church of the Beloved Disciple and affirmed its place within the wider sacramental tradition.

title: Archbishop Richard Arthur Marchenna in the Consecration Procession
description: Archbishop Richard Arthur Marchenna, Primate of the Old Roman Catholic Church in North America and principal consecrator of Bishop Robert Clement, walks between Father Leo (left) and Father John Darcy Noble (right) during the procession to the Church of the Beloved Disciple.

title: The Faithful Accompany Their New Bishop Home
description: Members of the congregation, clergy, and supporters follow behind the bishops as the procession makes its way from Metropolitan-Duane United Methodist Church to the Church of the Beloved Disciple after Bishop Clement's consecration. Led by processional crosses, flowers, and banners, the gathering transformed the streets of Greenwich Village into an extension of the liturgy, expressing the Church of the Beloved Disciple's conviction that sacramental life belonged not only within church walls but also in the public witness of a community claiming its place in both the Church and the city.

title: Official Portrait of Bishop Robert Mary Clement.
description: This official portrait of Bishop Robert Mary Clement was taken following his episcopal consecration on October 6, 1974, as Bishop of New York in the Eucharistic Catholic Church. Clothed in richly embroidered pontifical vestments, Clement is presented in the visual tradition of Catholic episcopal portraiture. The image marked the beginning of a new chapter in his ministry, one that combined apostolic succession with an unwavering commitment to providing sacramental ministry and pastoral care to LGBTQ Christians through the Church of the Beloved Disciple.

title: Brass Bishop's Crozier
description: This brass bishop's crozier served as the pastoral staff of Archbishop Robert Mary Clement throughout his episcopal ministry in the Church of the Beloved Disciple. Carried during pontifical liturgies, ordinations, sacred processions, and public demonstrations, the crozier became one of the most recognizable symbols of the church's apostolic ministry. Its richly ornamented head reflects medieval ecclesiastical craftsmanship while expressing the community's commitment to the continuity of historic Catholic tradition within an affirming ministry to LGBTQ Christians.

title: Crozier Head with the Agnus Dei
description: The crozier's elaborately worked volute centers on the Agnus Dei (Lamb of God) carrying the banner of the Resurrection, a traditional emblem of Christ's sacrificial death and triumph over death. The engraved brass is embellished with colored cabochons and scrolling foliate ornament, combining Gothic and Romanesque decorative motifs. As the principal symbol of the bishop's pastoral office, the crozier expressed Archbishop Clement's vocation as shepherd of the Church of the Beloved Disciple while proclaiming the resurrection hope that stood at the center of the community's sacramental life.

title: "New York's Gay Patriarch" on the Cover of FLASH
description: The cover of the June 15, 1976 issue of FLASH: The International Guide to Gay Living features Bishop Robert Mary Clement under the headline, "A Candid Interview with Bishop Robert Clement – New York's Gay Patriarch." Published during a period of increasing LGBTQ visibility following the Stonewall uprising, the magazine introduced Clement and the Church of the Beloved Disciple to a national LGBTQ readership. The feature reflected the church's growing prominence as one of the best-known sacramental ministries serving gay and lesbian Christians, highlighting Clement's conviction that LGBTQ people deserved full participation in the sacramental life of the Church without renouncing either their faith or their identity.

title: Dancers in the church 1
description: Interpretive dancers perform before the altar during the Easter liturgy at the Church of the Beloved Disciple. Organized through contacts of John Darcy Noble, the performance integrated movement, music, and worship, reflecting the congregation's openness to contemporary artistic expression within a traditional sacramental setting. The dance embodied themes of resurrection, joy, and spiritual renewal central to the Easter celebration. Takes place at the 348 West 14th street location.

title: Dancers in the church 2
description: Members of an interpretive dance ensemble offer a choreographed meditation during the Easter Eucharist as clergy look on from the sanctuary. Their expressive gestures transformed the church into a space where liturgy and the performing arts converged, inviting worshippers to experience the Easter proclamation through movement as well as word and sacrament. The ensemble was invited through the artistic connections of John Darcy Noble, whose interests helped broaden the church's liturgical life. Takes place at the 348 West 14th street location.

title: Dancers in the church 3
description: A dancer kneels before the altar during a liturgical performance presented as part of a special service at the Church of the Beloved Disciple. Throughout the 1970s, the congregation occasionally incorporated interpretive dance into its worship, drawing upon artists known to John Darcy Noble to explore themes of devotion, sacrifice, and resurrection through movement. These performances reflected the church's willingness to unite historic Catholic liturgy with contemporary forms of artistic and spiritual expression.

title: Church bulletin for anniversary service.
description: This commemorative bulletin was produced for the first anniversary of the dedication of the Church of the Beloved Disciple's permanent home and the first anniversary of Bishop Robert M. Clement's episcopal consecration. The service welcomed Bishop George A. Hyde, founder of the Eucharistic Catholic Church, as guest preacher and celebrated the congregation's remarkable transformation from a private house church, to public meetings in borrowed spaces into a thriving parish with its own church building. The bulletin reflects the community's understanding of these anniversaries as milestones in both its institutional history and its pioneering ministry to New York's gay community.

title: Archbishop George Augustine Hyde Preaching at the First Anniversary of Archbishop Clement's Consecration.
description: Archbishop George Augustine Hyde delivers the homily during the celebration of the first anniversary of Archbishop Robert Mary Clement's episcopal consecration at the Church of the Beloved Disciple in October 1975. Hyde, Archbishop of the Orthodox-Catholic Church of America and one of Clement's close allies, was the featured guest preacher for the anniversary liturgy. His presence affirmed the close relationship between the two bishops and highlighted the ecclesial heritage of the Church of the Beloved Disciple as a pioneering sacramental ministry serving LGBTQ Christians.

title: Portrait of George Augustine Hyde.
description: This restored portrait depicts the Rev. George Augustine Hyde shortly after the founding of the Eucharistic Catholic Church in Atlanta, Georgia, in 1946. Founded by Hyde, the church was the first documented Christian church in the United States to openly welcome homosexual men and women into its sacramental life without requiring celibacy or concealment. Hyde's pioneering ministry profoundly influenced the development of LGBTQ-affirming sacramental Christianity and laid the ecclesial foundation upon which later communities, including the Church of the Beloved Disciple, were built.

title: Seminarians of the Church of the Beloved Disciple
description: This photograph shows members of the Church of the Beloved Disciple's seminary gathered around the altar during a liturgical service in New York City in the late 1970s. The community developed a formal program of ministerial formation to prepare openly gay and lesbian memebrs of the church for ordained ministry within the Eucharistic Catholic tradition at a time when most Roman Catholic and Orthodox seminaries excluded homosexual candidates.

title: Acolytes of the Church of the Beloved Disciple
description: Two unidentified acolytes of the Church of the Beloved Disciple pose together before a liturgical service. Wearing white albs with red shoulder orphreys and crosses designed by the congregation, they represent the lay ministers who assisted at the church's Eucharistic celebrations and other sacramental rites. Although their names are unknown, photographs such as this document the indispensable role of volunteers whose service sustained the parish's worship and communal life.

title: Acolytes of the Church of the Beloved Disciple
description: Two unidentified acolytes of the Church of the Beloved Disciple pose together in white liturgical albs and simple wooden crosses before a service. The photograph preserves a rare glimpse of the congregation's lay ministry and the diverse community that participated in the church's liturgical life. While the individuals remain unidentified, they stand as representatives of the many members whose volunteer service helped shape the Church of the Beloved Disciple's distinctive and inclusive ministry.

title: Ordination of Five Priests for the Church of the Beloved Disciple
description: Bishop Robert Mary Clement ordains five priests for the Church of the Beloved Disciple during a liturgy in New York City on October 2, 1978. The ordinands—Fathers Mark, Paul, Victor, Gabriel, and Philip—were called to continue the church's ministry of serving LGBTQ Christians after having experienced rejection or exclusion from other Christian traditions. Their ordinations reflected the Church of the Beloved Disciple's commitment to cultivating an openly gay clergy and ensuring the continuity of its sacramental and pastoral mission.

title: "An Unusual Ordination"
description: Newspaper clipping from Our Town (October 22, 1978) describing the ordination of Fathers Mark, Paul, Victor, Gabriel, and Philip by Bishop Robert Mary Clement at the Church of the Beloved Disciple. The article recounts how the five men—many of whom had been denied ordination or ministry elsewhere because of their sexual orientation—found a vocation within the Church of the Beloved Disciple, where they were ordained to serve openly as priests. It provides a rare contemporary account of the congregation's inclusive theology and its pioneering role in the development of an openly LGBTQ Christian ministry.

title: Sacred Procession for Corpus Christi through Manhattan
description: Members of the Church of the Beloved Disciple carry a ceremonial canopy during a Corpus Christi procession through the streets of Manhattan. Beneath the canopy, clergy bore the Blessed Sacrament in a public witness to the Real Presence of Christ, continuing a centuries-old Catholic tradition in the heart of New York's gay community. For the congregation, such processions united sacramental devotion with public visibility, proclaiming that LGBTQ Christians belonged fully within the life and worship of the Church.

title: Corpus Christi Procession through Manhattan
description: Led by a processional cross, acolytes, and a canopy sheltering the Blessed Sacrament, members of the Church of the Beloved Disciple process through the streets of Manhattan on the Feast of Corpus Christi. The annual procession carried the Eucharist beyond the church walls into the public square, affirming both the Real Presence of Christ and the place of LGBTQ Christians within the Catholic sacramental tradition. Rain and city traffic did not deter the congregation, whose public witness united ancient devotional practice with the visibility and resilience of New York's gay community.

title: Palm Sunday Procession through Manhattan
description: Clergy, acolytes, and parishioners of the Church of the Beloved Disciple process through the streets of Manhattan on Palm Sunday, retracing Christ's entry into Jerusalem with prayer, hymns, and the processional cross. Led by Archbishop Robert M. Clement and the church's clergy, the procession carried the liturgy beyond the sanctuary, making the church's presence visible in the city's neighborhoods. For the congregation, these annual public processions affirmed both the continuity of Catholic tradition and the conviction that LGBTQ Christians belonged fully within the Church's sacramental life.

title: Procession for the Feast of the Assumption
description: Archbishop Robert M. Clement leads the Church of the Beloved Disciple's procession for the Feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary as clergy carry a flower-decked statue of the Virgin through the streets of Manhattan. By bringing one of the Church's principal Marian feasts into the public square, the congregation affirmed its deep devotion to Mary while demonstrating that LGBTQ Christians fully shared in the traditions of Catholic faith and worship. These annual processions expressed the Church of the Beloved Disciple's conviction that sacred ritual belonged not only within the sanctuary but also in the life of the city.

title: The Ordinary of the Mass.
description: These opening pages introduce the Ordinary of the Mass prepared by Clement for use at the Church of the Beloved Disciple. Drawing upon the ancient Gallican Rite of Saint Germain of Paris—known as the "Gothic Mass"—the booklet presents an English-language liturgy adapted from Latin and French sources while preserving the ceremonial richness of the Western Catholic tradition. The publication reflects Archbishop Robert M. Clement's commitment to rooting the church's pioneering LGBTQ ministry within the historic liturgical heritage of the Christian West.

title: Silver Chalice and Paten (image of historic use)
description: Designed by Fr. Leo Joseph, this silver chalice and paten were created for the liturgical use of the Church of the Beloved Disciple and became the congregation's principal Eucharistic vessels. The chalice is decorated with sacred figures and Christian symbols, reflecting the church's synthesis of Eastern and Western liturgical traditions. Used by Bishop Robert Mary Clement throughout the 1970s and 1980s. As one of the central liturgical objects of the Church of the Beloved Disciple, it symbolizes the community's understanding of the Eucharist as the living Christ made available to the LGBTQ community.

title: Silver Chalice and Paten (Present View)
description: The Church of the Beloved Disciple's silver chalice and paten, photographed in the present day, remain among the most significant surviving liturgical objects of the congregation. Designed by Fr. Leo Joseph around 1970, the hand-engraved silver vessels feature medallion portraits of Christ, the Virgin Mary, St. Robert, and St. Clement, together with eucharistic and ornamental motifs that reflect the church's synthesis of Eastern and Western Christian artistic traditions. For more than two decades they served as the principal Eucharistic vessels of the Church of the Beloved Disciple, used by Bishop Robert Mary Clement in the celebration of the Eucharist, holy unions, ordinations, and the liturgical year. Preserved today as part of the church's archival legacy, the chalice and paten embody the community's commitment to apostolic continuity, sacramental worship, and an affirming ministry to LGBTQ Christians, remaining enduring witnesses to one of the earliest openly gay-affirming sacramental communities in the United States.

title: Antimension Consecrated by Bishops George A. Hyde and Robert M. Clement
description: This Byzantine antimension is a consecrated liturgical cloth that serves as the bishop's authorization for the celebration of the Divine Liturgy. Depicting the Lamentation (Entombment) of Christ and inscribed in Church Slavonic with an English certification panel, it was consecrated and signed by Bishops George A. Hyde and Robert M. Clement on 5 October 1980. More than a devotional object, the antimension embodies episcopal authority and Eucharistic communion, documenting the close sacramental relationship between Hyde and Clement and the Church of the Beloved Disciple's appropriation of Byzantine liturgical tradition within an independent Orthodox-Catholic context.

title: Nativity Letter from Archbishop George Augustine Hyde
description: Christmas (Nativity) 1980 pastoral letter from Archbishop George Augustine Hyde of the Orthodox-Catholic Church of America addressed to Archbishop Robert Clement, Bishop John Darcy Noble, and Fr. Phillip of the Church of the Beloved Disciple and the Eucharistic Catholic Church. Written on the thirty-fourth anniversary of the founding of the Eucharistic Catholic Church, Hyde reflects on the church's pioneering ministry to gay Christians, recalling its origins in 1946 and its commitment to providing an affirming spiritual home for those excluded from other churches. Condemning efforts to deny homosexual persons access to the sacraments, he describes the Church of the Beloved Disciple as the continuing heir to the Eucharistic Catholic Church's mission and praises its clergy for faithfully carrying forward that apostolic ministry into a new generation.

title: Letter from Archbishop George Hyde on the Preservation of the Holy Eucharist Church Legacy
description: Two-page letter dated October 26, 1979, from Archbishop George Augustine Hyde of the Orthodox-Catholic Church of America to Bishop Robert Mary Clement of the Church of the Beloved Disciple. Hyde recounts the rediscovery of furnishings and devotional objects from the original Holy Eucharist Church in Atlanta, including wooden chairs, an altar cross, a Gospel Book, and his episcopal ring. He offers several of these artifacts to Clement for preservation, reflecting on their historical importance to the founding of the Eucharistic Catholic Church in 1946 and expressing his desire that its material and spiritual legacy continue through the ministry of the Church of the Beloved Disciple.

title: Original Holy Eucharist Church Altar
description: Photograph of the original altar of the Holy Eucharist Church in Atlanta, Georgia, showing the primitive altar cross, Gospel Book, and altar furnishings preserved from the congregation's earliest years. In a letter dated October 26, 1979, Archbishop George Augustine Hyde informed Bishop Robert Clement that these objects had been rediscovered after decades in storage and described their historical significance to the founding of the Eucharistic Catholic Church.

title: Original Holy Eucharist Church Chair
description: Photograph of one of the original wooden chairs used by the Holy Eucharist Church in Atlanta during its formative years. In his October 26, 1979 letter to Bishop Robert Clement, Archbishop George Augustine Hyde recounted the rediscovery of two such chairs after twenty-five years in storage and noted that they had furnished the congregation's earliest worship space.

title: Archbishops George Augustine Hyde and Richard Arthur Marchenna visiting the home of Robert Mary Clement and John Darcy Noble in New York City.
description: Hyde, Archbishop of the Orthodox-Catholic Church of America, and Marchenna, Primate of the Old Roman Catholic Church in North America, were both instrumental in providing apostolic succession and sacramental ministry to emerging independent Catholic communities. Their support of Robert Mary Clement and the Church of the Beloved Disciple helped establish it as one of the earliest ministries dedicated to providing full sacramental access to LGBTQ Christians.

title: Round Button with CBD Name and Logo
description: This small metal button bearing the name and emblem of the Church of the Beloved Disciple was produced as an identifying badge for members and supporters of the congregation. The design features the church's distinctive seal: a cross surrounding a Eucharistic chalice surmounted by the Sacred Host, accompanied by four stylized rosettes and the inscription "Church of the Beloved Disciple – Eucharistic Catholic." Worn at parish events, public processions, ecumenical gatherings, and LGBTQ demonstrations, the button served as a portable expression of the church's identity, publicly proclaiming both its sacramental tradition and its ministry of welcome and affirmation. Today it survives as a rare piece of material culture documenting one of America's earliest openly LGBTQ-affirming Catholic communities.

title: Round Button with CBD Logo
description: This small metal button reproduces the official emblem of the Church of the Beloved Disciple, presenting the congregation's distinctive visual identity without accompanying text. The design centers on a cross enclosing a Eucharistic chalice surmounted by the Sacred Host, symbolizing the centrality of the Eucharist in the church's theology and worship. Four stylized quatrefoils placed between the arms of the cross evoke both the four Evangelists and the universality of the Church. Distributed among members and supporters, the button was worn at liturgical celebrations, public processions, Pride marches, and ecumenical gatherings, serving as a recognizable symbol of the congregation's apostolic heritage and its public witness as one of the earliest openly LGBTQ-affirming sacramental churches in the United States.

title: Church Lapel Pin
description: This small enamel lapel pin reproduces the official emblem of the Church of the Beloved Disciple in the form of a cross. At its center, a Eucharistic chalice surmounted by the Sacred Host proclaims the church's sacramental identity, while four stylized quatrefoils occupy the spaces between the arms of the cross. Worn by clergy, members, and supporters, the pin served as a discreet yet recognizable expression of affiliation with the congregation. Its compact form made it suitable for everyday wear as well as for liturgical celebrations, public processions, ecumenical gatherings, and LGBTQ+ community events, embodying the church's distinctive witness as an openly affirming sacramental community rooted in Eucharistic devotion.

title: VIA January 1979
description: The January 1979 issue of The Eucharistic Catholic Via, the monthly newsletter of the Church of the Beloved Disciple, offers a vivid snapshot of parish life at the beginning of 1979. Published from the church's headquarters at 348 West 14th Street, New York City, the newsletter documents the congregation's liturgical life, theological vision, pastoral ministries, and engagement with the wider LGBTQ community. Articles report on Christmas celebrations, the annual St. Nicholas Fair, neighborhood crime-prevention efforts undertaken with Metropolitan-Duane Methodist Church and local organizations, and the church's memorial observances following the assassinations of San Francisco Mayor George Moscone and Supervisor Harvey Milk. The issue also inaugurates Fr. Mark Bradley's series On Being Gay and Christian, reflects on the church's understanding of Catholic identity and apostolic succession, and chronicles the community's expanding outreach, seminary, and public ministry. Together, the newsletter provides an invaluable contemporary record of the Church of the Beloved Disciple's religious, social, and civic life during a formative period in its history.

title: 8 page Brochure entitled "Church of the Beloved Disciple". 3.75" by 8.5" folded brochure
description: This illustrated brochure introduces the Church of the Beloved Disciple, presenting it as an independent Catholic congregation founded to provide a sacramental and affirming spiritual home for LGBTQ people at a time when few churches welcomed them. Through photographs and narrative, it traces the church's history from the founding of the Eucharistic Catholic Church by George Hyde in 1946 to Robert M. Clement's establishment of the Church of the Beloved Disciple in New York in 1970, highlighting milestones including the first public gay Catholic service in New York City, the acquisition of the church's own building, and the ordination and consecration of openly gay clergy. Produced as both a historical account and an invitation to worship, the brochure reflects the church's understanding of itself as an apostolic Catholic community that united traditional liturgy with LGBTQ religious affirmation and activism.

title: 6 page Brochure entitled "Come Alive Don't Suffocate in Spiritual Closets."3.75" by 8.5" folded brochure
description: This pamphlet encourages gay and lesbian Christians who feel alienated from their churches to embrace an affirming spiritual identity rather than remain, in its words, in "spiritual closets." It presents the Church of the Beloved Disciple as a sacramental Catholic community where LGBTQ people could worship openly and fully, arguing that gay identity is a God-given gift and calling for the creation and support of LGBTQ-led churches. Combining theological reflection with an invitation to membership, the brochure illustrates the church's mission to unite traditional Catholic worship with the emerging gay liberation movement of the 1970s.

title: Opening Pages of Bishop John Darcy Noble's Consecration Service Booklet
description: The opening pages of the official program for the Ceremony of Consecration of The Most Reverend John Joseph Noble, D.D. as Bishop Coadjutor of New York of the Eucharistic Catholic Church, held at Metropolitan-Duane Church, New York City, on Sunday, October 5, 1980. The booklet includes Bishop Noble's official portrait, the order of service, and the names of the principal participants, including Archbishop Robert M. Clement, who served as consecrator, and Archbishop George A. Hyde, Primate of the Orthodox Catholic Church of America, who served as co-consecrator. The service booklet reflects the continuity of apostolic succession within the Church of the Beloved Disciple and the enduring relationship between Clement's ministry and the ecclesiastical lineage established by George Augustine Hyde more than three decades earlier.

title: Letter of Episcopal Recognition for John Darcy Noble
description: Letter issued by Bishop Alfred Louis (Lankenau), Chancellor of the Orthodox-Catholic Church of America, recognizing the canonical election of John Darcy Noble to the episcopate and consenting to his consecration on October 5, 1980 by Archbishop George Augustine Hyde and Bishop Robert Mary Clement. Dated October 2, 1980, the document evidences the Orthodox-Catholic Church of America's recognition of Noble's elevation as the second bishop of the Church of the Beloved Disciple.

title: Bishop John Darcy Noble
description: Photograph of Bishop John Darcy Noble (1923–2003) in episcopal vestments holding his crozier, taken during or shortly after his consecration and enthronement as the second bishop of the Church of the Beloved Disciple on October 5, 1980. A founding member of the Church of the Beloved Disciple, Noble helped continue the church's ministry of sacramental worship, pastoral care, and advocacy for LGBTQ Christians throughout the 1980s.

title: Easter Sermon 1982 - Archbishop Clement Easter
description: A restored recording of Archbishop Robert Mary Clement's Easter Day sermon, preached at the Church of the Beloved Disciple on April 11, 1982. Speaking to a predominantly lesbian and gay congregation, Clement proclaimed the Resurrection as the triumph of life over fear and exclusion, affirming that "God lives. God is alive. God is present with us—for each one of us. Straight or gay. This is God's house. God's love. God's church. God's people." The sermon exemplifies the church's theology of radical inclusion, emphasizing Christ's message of abundant life, the dignity of LGBTQ+ people, and the Eucharist as the living sign of God's unconditional love. Restored from the original audio recording.

title: Bishop Clement and Ravarour celebrating Mass in Los Angeles (circa 2010)
description: One of the last known photographs of Bishop Robert Mary Clement at the altar, concelebrating the Eucharist with Bishop Ravarour in Los Angeles around 2010. Although the Church of the Beloved Disciple NYC had ceased to exist as an active parish decades earlier, Clement continued to exercise his priestly ministry, preserving the liturgical traditions and sacramental vision that had defined the church since its founding. The image stands as a poignant testament to the continuity of his vocation and his lifelong commitment to an inclusive Catholic ministry.

title: Archbishop Robert Mary Clement at Los Angeles Pride 2008
description: Archbishop Robert Mary Clement smiles during the Los Angeles Pride Parade on June 8, 2008, nearly four decades after carrying a sign proclaiming "Gay People, This Is Your Church" at New York's first Christopher Street Liberation Day March in 1970. Surrounded by members of an interfaith clergy contingent, Clement remained a visible public witness for LGBTQ+ inclusion in Christianity throughout his life. His presence at Pride reflected the enduring mission of the Church of the Beloved Disciple: to proclaim that LGBTQ+ people are fully embraced within the life of the Church and the sacramental love of God.

title: Senior Prom: LGBTQ+ Seniors Get the Prom of Their Dreams | PBS Short Docs
description:
Description: "Senior Prom" takes on a whole new meaning at Triangle Square, a haven for LGBTQ+ retirees in Hollywood, CA. For so many high-schoolers, prom is a rite of passage in all of its love-filled, well-coiffed, abundantly photographed glory. But for generations of LGBTQ+ youth, prom has been emblematic of exclusion from a world they could not experience as their authentic selves. Over a night of dancing, kissing, and crowning of prom queens at Triangle Square, these trailblazing seniors reflect back on how far they've come and their dreams for the next generation. “Senior Prom” celebrates our eldest LGBTQ+ generation who spent a lifetime fighting for the right to love openly and, via rich personal archives, retraces lives and legacies of resistance that helped change the course of civil rights.
Segments with Robert: 02:26-02:49; 06:57-08:53; 11:37-13:00

title: Rev. Robert Clement 100th Birthday Tribute
description: This video tribute was first presented at LGBTQ-RAN's Passionate Prophets GALA in 2024. Clement is perhaps most noted for founding The Church of the Beloved Disciple in Manhattan (1968-1986), the first major church for the LGBT community in New York and being co-creator of the term “Holy Union” when he presided over a same-sex wedding ceremony at his church in July 1970.
